[CALPHAD: Computer Coupling of Phase Diagrams and Thermochemistry 71 (2020) 102203](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.calphad.2020.102203)

Assessment of diffusion mobility for bcc phase of Ti–Al–Ni ternary system 

Qiaojun Wu, Guanglong Xu, Hui Chang, Lian Zhou, Yuwen Cui \* 

*Tech Institute of Advanced Materials & School of Materials Science and Engineering, Nanjing Tech University, Nanjing, 211816, China*   

A R T I C L E I N F O  	A B S T R A C T  

| *Keywords:*  Diffusion mobility bcc phase  Ti–Al–Ni ternary Alloys  Ti–Ni binary  DICTRA  Phenomenological treatment  | The experimental diffusion coefficients of the Ti–Ni binary and Ti–Al–Ni ternary bcc phase were critically evaluated to assess the diffusion mobilities by the DICTRA-type phenomenological treatment. The calculated diffusion coefficient shows reasonable consistency with the diffusion coefficient extracted in the experiment, including the impurity and inter-diffusion coefficients in bcc Ti–Ni binary alloy and the main interdiffusion coefficient in bcc Ti–Al–Ni ternary alloy. The difference between the calculated and experimental ternary cross coefficients is within appropriate relative errors. The predicted composition profiles and diffusion paths reasonably represent the diffusion processes that occur in Ti–Ni binary and Ti–Al–Ni ternary diffusion couples, thereby validating the mobility database assessed in the present work.    |
| :---- | :---- |

1. # **Introduction** 

Titanium alloys are increasingly applied in aerospace, automotive and biomedical fields due to their excellent specific strength, superior corrosion resistance and biocompatibility, etc \[1\]. The β-stabilizer Ni has been widely utilized as a solid-solution strengthening element in titanium alloys, often collaborating with Al, Mo and/or Zr, to improve the mechanical properties and corrosion resistance \[2,3\]. It is well known that microstructure features and mechanical properties of structural metallic materials are largely affected by recrystallization, phase transformation, and grain growth process, and much of these processes are essentially governed by diffusion interactions \[4\]. Therefore, diffusion properties and kinetics are of fundamental importance to understanding the influence of alloying additions, optimizing the heat treatment parameters, and designing the microstructure for the target alloys. It is in two excellent handbooks \[5,6\] that available diffusion coefficients for Ti-based binaries (and many other binary alloys) were comprehensively surveyed and tabulated, whereas the study of diffusion in Ti–Al-X ternary alloys is relatively new, sparse and scattered on the journals in metallic materials \[7–16\]. 

In recent years, the DICTRA-type (diffusion-controlled transformation) \[17\] phenomenological treatment has emerged as an efficient computational tool to evaluate the reliability and mutual compatibility of experimental diffusion data and develop the diffusion kinetic database. Also called as computational diffusion kinetics \[18\], it can be used to perform the simulation of diffusion behaviors and diffusion-controlled processes, such as micro-segregation during solidification, homogenization kinetics, growth/dissolution kinetics of precipitates, in conjunction with the corresponding thermodynamic database. 

Up to now, there are mobility databases available for aluminum alloy systems \[19,20\], steels \[21\], and nickel-base alloy systems \[22\], and so on. As for Ti-based alloys, the database for Ti/TiAl-based alloys through the Thermo-Calc AB \[23\] is commercially available, which covers some Ti/TiAl-based alloys. In recent years, a series of studies on the diffusion kinetics in Ti–Al-X ternaries (inc. Cr, Fe, Mn, Mo, Nb, Sn, Zr, and V, etc) \[13,24–30\] have been carried out in the authors’ group. As a part of the serial work, the diffusion experiment of bcc Ti–Al–Ni ternary alloys has been investigated by utilizing ternary diffusion couples \[12\], which makes possible to evaluate this new ternary diffusion research by jointly inspecting the diffusion in Ti–Ni binary and to assess the atomic mobility for the Ti–Al–Ni ternary. Meanwhile, it is noticed that Wang et al. \[31\] performed a DICTRA-type assessment to develop the atomic mobility of bcc Ti–Ni alloys. However, the interdiffusion coefficients employed in their assessment show a peculiar compositional dependence that considerably differs from others. Hence, there is a need to reassess the diffusion behaviors in bcc Ti–Ni binary alloys.

Accordingly, the present work aims to: (i) critically evaluate the measured diffusion data of bcc Ti–Ni and Ti–Al–Ni alloys from the literature; (ii) reassess the diffusion mobility of the bcc phase of Ti–Ni binary; (iii) assess the mobility of the bcc phase of Ti–Al–Ni ternary; and (iv) predict the composition profiles and diffusion paths occurring in Ti–Ni binary and Ti–Al–Ni ternary diffusion couples and compare with experimentally measured values to validate the mobility assessed in this work.

3. # **Evaluation of the experimental data** 

The tracer, impurity, and interdiffusion coefficients for the bcc phase in Ti–Ni and Al–Ni and Ti–Al–Ni systems showed some inconsistency among reported works. It is necessary to evaluate all the experimental data from an overall viewpoint of diffusional kinetics. 

1. ## *The Ti*–*Ni binary* 

Peart and Tomlin \[35\] measured the tracer diffusion coefficients of Ni in pure bcc-Ti at the temperatures from 1209 K to 1511 K using the isotope 63Ni by means of the standard serial sectioning method. Gibbs et al. \[36\] determined the impurity diffusion coefficients of 63Ni in bcc-Ti at the temperatures ranging from 1220 K to 1991 K. Taking these two sets of experimental data \[35,36\] into account, the Ni diffusion in bcc-Ti was approximated by a two-exponent form expression \[37\], describing the abnormal diffusion of Ni in bcc-Ti that follows a strong curved Arrhenius relation. The two sets of data were included and given equal weights to assess the atomic mobility of Ni in bcc-Ti. 

Bastin et al. \[38\] determined the interdiffusion coefficients of bcc Ti–Ni solid solution within the temperature ranging from 1073 K to 1213 K by fabricating the Ti/Ti–TiNi3 and Ti/Ti–TiNi diffusion couples, respectively. A majority of the experimental coefficients show a gradual upward trend as the Ni content increases, while a few others show a weak dependence on the Ni content. Shevchuk \[39\] measured the interdiffusion coefficients of the bcc Ti–Ni alloys at the temperatures of

1173 K, 1323 K and 1523 K. Those coefficients were extracted by the Matano method. However, those results are quite scattering and seemingly decrease rapidly with increasing the Ni content, which have not been adopted in the assessment. In a recent study, Wang et al. \[31\] fabricated the Ti/Ti-6 at.% Ni diffusion couples and extracted the interdiffusion coefficients at the temperatures of 1273, 1373, and 1473 K in terms of the Den Broeder scheme \[40\]. However, with the increase of Ni content, the decrease of the interdiffusion coefficient deviates from what is suggested by the monotonically decreasing bcc solidus at the Ni-rich part of the Ti–Ni phase diagram. Moreover, as the solute composition approaches zero, an extrapolation to the Ti end of the interdiffusion coefficients yields the Ni impurity diffusivity in bcc-Ti. By doing this, the extrapolated impurity diffusion coefficients in Ref. \[31\] profoundly differ from the others \[35,36\], particularly for 1273 K and 1373 K. Therefore, a re-extraction of the impurity and interdiffusion coefficients in bcc Ti–Ni alloys is required. To this end, the error function expansion (ERFEX) \[11,41\] was utilized to smooth and represent the accessible EPMA data in Ref. \[31\] in an analytical expression of

Thereafter, the Sauer- Freise method \[42\] and Hall method \[43\] were respectively utilized to extract impurity and interdiffusion coefficients. All other interdiffusion data apart from Shevchuk’s, were selected and assigned with certain weights in the optimization process. 

2. ## *The Al*–*Ni binary* 

According to the accepted Al–Ni phase diagram \[44\], the disordered bcc phase (bcc\_A2 phase) in the binary system is unstable, so there is no experimental data for diffusion. The diffusion coefficients and atomic mobility for the bcc\_A2 phase can only be accessible as a disordered part (as suggested by Girifalco \[45\]) of the order B2\_bcc phase of the Al–Ni

binary \[46,47\]. Helander and Ågren \[46\] assumed that the mobilities of Al and Ni in bcc-Al and bcc-Ni were the same as the mobility of bcc-Fe, while Wei et al. \[47\] tried to gauge those parameters directly from the experimental diffusion coefficients of bcc\_B2 by splitting off the contribution of the ordered part. Unfortunately, the resulting mobilities of the disorder bcc Al and Ni by Wei et al. are extremely unphysical small, as Table 1 shows, more than 10 orders of magnitude smaller than the others. In fact, Liu et al. \[48\] commented that the parameters of Wei et al. \[47\] were not suitable to a multicomponent database. In contrast, the diffusion coefficient obtained using the parameters of Helander and Ågren \[46\] shows an order of magnitude between − 9 and − 16, which is comparable to the results of semi-empirical calculations \[31,49\] and ab-initio machine learning Method \[50\]. Therefore, the mobility parameters of Helander and Ågren \[46\] were directly used in the current work. 

3. ## *The Ti*–*Al*–*Ni ternary* 

The interdiffusion behaviors in the bcc phase of Ti–Al–Ni ternary alloys at 1473 K have been investigated \[12\] by conducting the solid-state diffusion couple experiments. With the help of ERFEX-based smoothing and fitting, the interdiffusion coefficients were extracted utilizing the Green-Whittle method \[51\]. All the interdiffusion coefficients satisfy the justified thermodynamic constraints \[52\]. In this work, the experimental main coefficients were adopted to optimize the ternary interaction mobility parameters, whereas the cross coefficients were taken only for comparisons because they show some scattering data and improper change of the sign within a limited composition range. 

4. # **Optimization procedure** 

The optimization of atomic mobility requires a reliable thermodynamic description to provide thermodynamic factors in diffusion. For Ti–Al–Ni ternary system, the widely accepted thermodynamic parameters by Dupin \[53\] were utilized in this work. 

The mobility of Ti self-diffusion assessed by Chen et al. \[54\] was admitted in this work because it better represents the non-linear Arrhenius relation of bcc-Ti self-diffusion than that of Liu et al. \[55\]. The mobility parameters of the Ti–Al binary were based on the work of Li et al. \[25\]. All the other parameters were optimized by fitting to the selected experimental data via the DICTRA software. The optimization process is as follows: 1\) the parameter *QTiNi* was optimized by fitting to the Ni impurity diffusivities in bcc-Ti; 2\) the interaction parameters 0*QTiNi,Ni*, 1*QTiNi,Ni*, 0*QTiTi ,Ni* and 1*QTiTi ,Ni* were then obtained to describe the bcc Ti–Ni interdiffusion coefficients; 3\) and the ternary interaction parameters, 

0*QNi,Ti*, 0*QAlNi,Ti*, 1*QAlNi ,Ti* and 0*QAlTi ,Ni* were assessed with the experimental 

*Al*

ternary main interdiffusion coefficients. All the assessed mobility parameters of the bcc Ti–Al–Ni ternary are listed in Table 2.

2. ## *The Ti*–*Al*–*Ni system* 

The diffusion mobilities of bcc Ti–Al–Ni ternary alloy were assessed by fitting to the selected experimental interdiffusion coefficients. Table 3 presents the calculated and experimental main interdiffusion coefficients (*D*˜*TiAlAl* and *D*˜*TiNiNi*) at 1473 K. Fig. 3 compares the calculated main interdiffusion coefficients with the experiment values on a logarithmic scale. The linear regression of the data along the solid line with a slope of 1 indicates a nice agreement between the experiment and calculated values. The red dashed lines display the 25% error tolerance lines between experiments and assessment. In this work, 90% of *D*˜*TiAlAl* and *D*˜*TiNiNi* lie within the prediction interval. The errors are less than the widely accepted uncertainty of experimental diffusion coefficients 

### **Table 3** 

±50% \[29,57\], which implies the reliability of the main diffusion coefficients. 

Table 4 presents the values of cross interdiffusion coefficients (*D*˜*TiAlNi* and *D*˜*TiNiAl*) at 1473 K. It is apparent that all the calculated *D*˜*TiAlNi* exhibits a negative sign, i.e. Al uphill diffusion against the gradient of Ni composition with Ti as the reference specie. Most of *D*˜*TiNiAl* values are positive with an exception of certain alloys with a chemical composition very close to the Ti terminal. The calculated cross interdiffusion coefficients were indirectly derived by best representing all the experimental finding in a self-consistent way. For this reason, the deviation between experiment and calculation seems to be more obvious. In fact, this is also because the cross coefficient is more susceptible to the shape or trajectory of the component distribution map than the main term \[58\], which may bring greater uncertainty to the extraction of the cross term. 

Fig. 4 presents the 3D plot of the calculated ternary interdiffusion coefficients, impurity diffusion coefficients *D*\**Al*(*Ti*− *Ni*) and *D*\**Ni*(*Ti*− *Al*), together with the binary interdiffusion coefficients *D*˜*Ti*− *Al* and *D*˜*Ti*− *Ni*. Note that as the Ni content increases, the main interdiffusion coefficient *D*˜*TiAlAl* increases significantly, which indicates that the addition of Ni promotes the diffusion of Al in bcc Ti–Al–Ni alloys. On the contrary, the main coefficient *D*˜*TiNiNi* is greatly reduced with the increase of Al content,

6. # **Validation by diffusion simulations** 

The validation of the obtained diffusion mobility includes not only the comparison with the experimental diffusion coefficients but also the comparison between the predicted and observed diffusion behaviors in diffusion experiments, especially like composition profiles and diffusion paths. In conjunction with the thermodynamic description for the Ti–Al–Ni ternary, the mobility parameters developed in this work can be utilized to virtually perform diffusion experiments and predict interesting diffusion phenomena occurring in diffusion couples. 

Fig. 5 shows the verification for the Ti–Ni binary system. The composition profiles of the Ti/Ti-6 at.% Ni diffusion couple after annealing at 1273 K for 14 h and 1473 K for 4 h were presented. The solid curve is the calculation result, and the experimental points \[31\] are superimposed for comparison. This agreement is satisfactory for most experimental measurements, and further confirms the reliability of the mobility parameters evaluated by the bcc Ti–Ni binary system. 

Fig. 6 shows the diffusion paths at 1473 K for all ternary diffusion couples. The solid curves are calculation results based on the present diffusion mobility. The relevant experimental data are marked in different symbols for comparison. The composition-distance profiles for individual ternary diffusion couples are also calculated and provided in the supplementary materials. Overall, the simulated diffusion path reproduces the results detected by EPMA well. Note that the end of most S- shaped paths tends to be parallel to the direction at the Al constant content, suggesting that the diffusion of Ni is much faster than that of Al. Although it is found that the EPMA data is scattered in the D3, D4 and T4 measurements, and the diffusion behavior of D6 away from the Ti end might be affected by the complex interaction between the elements, the simulated diffusion paths have an essential S-shaped feature as other diffusion paths exhibit. Additional attempts have been made to fit the above profiles strictly. It would deteriorate the overall agreement between experiment and simulation. Taking into account large uncertainty in diffusion-couple experiment, the deviation between the EPMA data and the simulated path in the current version is acceptable. 

7. # **Conclusion** 

The diffusion mobilities for the bcc Ti–Ni binary and Ti–Al–Ni ternary alloys were assessed by fitting to the evaluated experimental diffusion data through the DICTRA software. Reasonable agreements were obtained from comprehensive comparisons between calculated and experimental interdiffusion coefficients. The developed mobility database, in conjunction with the CALPHAD-based thermodynamic descriptions, has been successfully utilized to predict such diffusion properties as composition profiles and diffusion paths for the Ti–Ni binary and Ti–Al–Ni ternary diffusion couples.
